Subject: Catalyst pilot - private deploy networking options

Hi Irene / Kimberly,

Thanks again for the quick sync earlier. We're getting the Catalyst pilot ready and need to lock the networking approach for the private deployment (we plan to host the model in our VPC but use Redwood Private control plane). High-level constraints from our side:

- Must meet SOC 2 / HIPAA-style evidence gating for access and auditability.
- Target median request latency < 60ms (US-east client footprint), 95th < 200ms.
- Expected sustained egress from our VPC: ~120 req/s during business hours, burst to 400 req/s. Average payload ~1.2k tokens per request.
- We have on-prem legacy systems that will still need access via a site-to-site VPN; we may want a single ingress that covers both cloud and on-prem traffic.
- Operationally, we prefer a low-op model: a managed endpoint is better than running customer-facing VPNs if security/compliance and latency are acceptable.

Attached is our network spec (Harbor_Catalyst_Network_Specs.pdf). Can you outline trade-offs between VPC peering, interface endpoints (PrivateLink), and an IPsec S2S VPN for this exact profile? Also: what measurable differences should we expect on cost and failover?

Appreciate a short write-up we can share with our infra/compliance reviewers. Happy to set a 30-min workshop if helpful.

Best,
Sam Ortega
Director of Cloud Platforms
Harbor Health

Folks — I pulled together a concise trade-off analysis for the Catalyst numbers. See bullets below and a proposed pilot architecture (recommendation + fallback). I attached a short cheatsheet (redwood-connectivity-cheatsheet.pdf) with operational MOPs.

Summary (quick):
- VPC peering: lowest latency (L3 direct routing) if both parties run in same cloud and same region/account constraints permit. Not cross-account-friendly for private-provider model; requires route table management and can expose broad surface area if not carefully scoped. Good for high-throughput, minimal rtt overhead.

- PrivateLink (AWS Interface Endpoint): strong security isolation (only specific service interfaces reachable), good cross-account model, easier allowlisting (ENIs per AZ). Slight per-packet latency overhead vs peering (typically +2–10ms) but predictable. Operationally managed; Redwood can publish service name and Harbor creates VPC Endpoint — low-maintenance. Cost: per-ENI/hour + per-GB data processing; simplifies compliance scoping because access is only to specific service.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): necessary for on-prem -> cloud connectivity. Flexible (works with on-prem and multi-cloud), but significantly higher latency and jitter versus cloud-native options. Requires lifecycle ops (tunnels, key rotation, monitoring). Can be used as a backup path or to reach legacy resources. If you need deterministic sub-100ms for US-east clients, IPsec may struggle depending on last-mile.

Micro-decision factors for your constraints (120 req/s sustained, bursts to 400, median <60ms):
- Primary path: PrivateLink into Redwood Private running in Harbor's VPC (or a partner VPC) — satisfies compliance (limited exposure), low operational burden, predictable latency. Expect 95th percentiles in your target assuming region co-location; overhead is small vs peering.
- Backup path: IPsec S2S tunnel from Harbor edge to Redwood edge cluster for on-prem failover and legacy-system access. Use policy-based routing or health checks to prefer PrivateLink and cut over to IPsec when PrivateLink health fails.
- Peering only makes sense if Redwood components are deployed in the exact same VPC/account and you can accept the broader surface area and routing management. Given Harbor's compliance needs, PrivateLink is more audit-friendly.

Operational recommendations:
1) Pilot with PrivateLink + IPsec backup in two AZs. Validate 95th latency and token-based egress costs in the pilot window.
2) Configure endpoint-specific logging (flow logs on ENIs, VPC flow logs aggregated to a secure S3) and enable token-level auditing in the Redwood Console so you can map requests back to users.
3) Create a small mutual action plan (MAP) with these milestones: endpoint provisioning, IPsec config, smoke test (latency + failover), SOC artifact exchange.

Cost note: expected data processing charges for PrivateLink are modest at your scale (~$0.02–0.06/GB depending on transfer profile) but per-ENI hour does add up if you require dedicated ENIs in many AZs. We'll include a rough estimate after we see your traffic CSV.

Next steps I recommend:
- Sam: share your 95th token size and the CIDR/IP allowlist constraints (if any).
- We'll run a 48-hour perf pilot (PrivateLink primary, IPsec backup) and produce latency/cost numbers and an operations runbook.

—Ben Carter
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
(attachment: redwood-connectivity-cheatsheet.pdf)

Thanks Ben — helpful summary. Some answers and follow-ups from Harbor infra/compliance:

- Final answer on hosting: we expect Redwood Private to run within our AWS account (Harbor will provide an account/OU that runs the inference nodes). We still want the managed service feel for connectivity (i.e., minimal ops on our side).
- 95th token size: 2.6k tokens (this includes some rare long-form requests).
- Traffic mix: ~85% synchronous single-request flows; ~15% streaming for longer transcripts.
- Egress allowlist: we prefer to lock down to service-specific endpoints rather than open peering.

We attached a small traffic profile (catalyst_traffic_profile.csv) and a procurement doc asking for SLA/pricing details (request_sla_pricing.docx). Also: please share SOC2 evidence (summary) and any notes about where audit logs will live and retention windows.

Can you include a brief proposed ConfigSpec for the PrivateLink endpoint and the IPsec tunnels (BGP vs static, MTU, health probing)? Compliance will want concrete port/IP details we can insert into our change ticket.

Regards,

From: irene.choi@redwood.com <irene.choi@redwood.com>
To: Sam Ortega <sam.ortega@harborhealth.com>, Liu Zhang <liu.zhang@harborhealth.com>
Cc: ben.carter@redwood.com, kimberly.park@redwood.com
Date: Thu, 20 May 2026 16:04:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Catalyst pilot - ingress strategy evaluation and multipath fallback proposal

Sam / Liu — thanks for the data. Based on Harbor's hosting model (Redwood Private deployed in your AWS account) and the traffic profile, our recommendation is the following pilot configuration:

1) Primary: AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint) per AZ to the Redwood Private service in Harbor's account. ConfigSpec (summary):
   - ENIs in each AZ, SGs limited to Harbor app subnets, explicit allowlist to Redwood service ENIs.
   - MTU: 9001 where possible; fall back to 1500 for legacy on-prem systems.
   - Health: use active TCP health probes (we will provide a health endpoint) + VPC endpoint status checks.
   - Logging: enable VPC Flow Logs -> secure S3; enable Redwood request logs at token-level (retention 90 days by default).

2) Backup / Legacy access: IPsec S2S tunnels to Redwood edge (two tunnels primary/secondary) with static routing for simplicity on the first pilot. ConfigSpec (summary):
   - IPsec: AES-GCM, SHA2, IKEv2, PFS group 14.
   - Routing: static for pilot (we'll surface BGP as next step if you need dynamic failover).
   - MTU: 1500, with MSS clamping for HTTP streaming.
   - Failover: health-check + routing policy to prefer PrivateLink; automatic failover to IPsec on PrivateLink health failures.

3) Compliance/artifacts: we'll share a SOC2 summary (attached) and provide a runbook showing where logs are stored and TTLs. For the MAP, we'll own the PrivateLink provisioning instructions and provide a config bundle Harbor can use in the change ticket.

4) Pilot timeline & action items (target: 2 weeks pilot):
   - Day 0–2: Harbor to open change ticket and create endpoint subnets; share allowlist and role for endpoint creation.
   - Day 3–5: Redwood to provide CloudFormation template & IPsec config snippets; Harbor to provision endpoints and S2S tunnels.
   - Day 6–8: Smoke tests (latency / token integrity / failover exercise).
   - Day 9–14: Collect metrics, produce latency/cost/ops report and recommended steady-state.

Attachments: I uploaded a draft MAP and the implementation checklist for the PrivateLink+IPsec pilot. Please review and confirm the timeline; if Harbor prefers dynamic routing for the tunnels we can swap to BGP on Day 5 but it'll add ~2–3 days to validation.

I will schedule a 30-min workshop Friday 10am PST to walk Harbor infra through the CloudFormation and IPsec snippets.

—Irene Choi
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
irene.choi@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0199
